samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cite the actual duplicated values well, but A gives concrete target scales (spacing 4–48, radius 4/8/12, control height 40). It also justifies the migration order by how visible each change is, and states its assumptions. B is tighter and calls out the shadows more clearly, but it gives counts instead of target values and states as fact that the input and select sit side by side. A has a stray '[count from your repo]' placeholder, and neither answer explicitly separates intentional differences from accidental ones. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers quote the actual values well and catch the same near-duplicates. B is stronger where the rubric matters most: it proposes concrete scales (spacing 4–48, radius 4/8/12, control height 40), orders the migration from least to most visible change, and says which merges will be invisible and which will shift layouts. B is longer, includes a stray '[count from your repo]' placeholder, and claims without evidence that 'the real numbers will be worse', while A is more concise but never gives target values.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers quote the specific duplicate values and give a sensible plan: audit, then scales, then tokens, then migration, then lint. A explicitly maps each existing value onto its proposed scale, which shows what will visibly shift. It also keeps the modal as a separate overlay elevation and hedges its contrast estimate and its chunk-only counts. B is slightly tighter and adds useful time estimates and lint rule names, but it calls the modal shadow a one-off instead of a possibly intentional elevation. It also says less about the limits of seeing only one excerpt. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers find the same near-duplicate colors, radii, control heights and spacing from the CSS, and both give a sensible audit, tokens, migrate, lint order. B is better: it maps each existing value onto a target scale, says plainly that small visible shifts will happen, and keeps the overlay elevation separate instead of flattening it. B also hedges its contrast estimate and states that its counts come from this chunk only. A is tighter and easier to scan, but it is less specific about the mappings and about which differences might be intentional.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A covers more of the CSS's actual causes, including the near-twin card and panel shadows, and gives a full merge map from old values to new ones. It is also more careful about what it can't see: it says its contrast figure is unchecked and an estimate, and it keeps the modal's elevation and a possible card/panel difference instead of flattening them. B is solid and mentions layout shifts and screenshot diffs, but it states contrast failure and side-by-side usage as fact and says to snap every value without separating accidental from intentional differences. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B quotes every drifted value, shadows included, and gives an explicit merge map. It keeps intentional differences: the modal elevation stays, and card/panel merge only if they don't behave differently. It also explains its step order and hedges the contrast estimate. A is tighter and accurate, but it says to snap every value without separating accidental from intentional differences, and it states contrast and usage claims with more confidence than one excerpt supports.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers open by calling the set sound, then pile on many new tokens and scales the team didn't ask for, which goes against the rubric's preference for few, targeted changes. A is noticeably shorter and suggests fewer additions. B goes further, adding info, on-status, raised and sunken surfaces, border-width and longer-duration tokens, though it hedges its contrast numbers more consistently. A's tighter scope makes it the better sanity pass, even though it states 'contrast is solid' as fact before admitting the ratios were estimated by hand. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers turn a sanity pass into a long list of new tokens, which goes against the rubric's preference for few, justified changes. B opens with a clearer verdict ('in good shape'), keeps only four must-fix items, and is somewhat shorter, though it states that contrast passes before hedging later. A has more numbered fixes and more speculative additions (on-* pairs, info, raised and sunken surfaces, border widths, a longer duration), even though its contrast caveats are more consistent.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers miss the brief's restraint goal. Each lists more than a dozen changes and adds many speculative tokens, when the set mostly needed a confirmation plus a few small gaps (focus ring, strong border, disabled state). B wins narrowly: its opening verdict names why the set is coherent, and it flags its contrast numbers as estimates to verify up front. A states the border WCAG failure as fact. B loses points for suggesting a `--ty-` prefix, which would rename every token, and for adding a governance section. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers open by calling the set coherent, but each then proposes a large expansion, with many speculative tokens and a long list of items. A is tighter and flags its contrast numbers as hand estimates to verify, though it still suggests a `--ty-` prefix that would rename every existing token. B is longer, states the border's WCAG failure as fact, and pushes even more additions (a rem conversion, extra spacing and type steps, easing curves, surface-elevation tokens), so it strays further from a light sanity pass.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers call the set solid but then list a dozen or more additions, so neither fits the request for a light sanity pass. A is shorter, renames no existing tokens and reprints nothing, although it states contrast ratios as fact. B is better at flagging its contrast numbers and proposed values as things to verify, but it is much longer, includes a large code block and proposes renaming --text-* to --font-size-*. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers call the set solid, then pile on many additions, so neither takes a restrained sanity-pass approach. A proposes renaming `--text-*` to `--font-size-*`, prints a large block of new tokens, and has more must-fix items, though it hedges its contrast claims better. B keeps the existing names, is somewhat shorter and offers a patch rather than printing one. But B states AA contrast as fact, and it adds speculative scopes such as z-index, scrim and breakpoints.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer B adds a specific date, 'October 17', that wasn't in the request. Answer A uses only the facts given and has clear When and Where cards, but its info cards overlap the end of the hero tagline, which looks broken. Neither screenshot shows the volunteer section, and neither shows any CSS, so rubric items 2 and 4 can't be checked properly; those scores are partly assumed. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Answer A looks clean and warm, but it gives the date as 'Saturday, October 17'. That date was invented, and it is wrong: today is October 27, so 'next Saturday' is October 31. A wrong date on an event page breaks rubric item 1. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both pages use only the facts given and are warm and restrained, and neither shows padding or invented details in the visible part. A puts the date and place in clear, full-width stacked cards that read well and should hold up on a phone. B's three-column info strip squeezes the address into an awkward three-line wrap and is more likely to get cramped on a narrow screen. Only the top of each page was visible, so I couldn't check the volunteer section or the CSS, and those scores are estimates. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): The two pages look much alike: warm cream and burgundy colours, system serif fonts, and the same 'What's on the tables' section with pill tags. B makes the date and place easier to read, with full-width When and Where rows, while A squeezes the address into a narrow third column where it wraps awkwardly and the info card sits right against the header. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick a 4px base with about a 1.2 ratio, give numbers a developer could use, and treat Tailwind fairly: take its spacing, skip its type scale. A edges ahead because it is tighter and its tablet values suit gloves better (56px rows, 12–16px gaps). It also adds practical rules: tabular numerals, and choosing density with `pointer: coarse` rather than viewport width. B has the more deliberate token set with named roles, but it runs longer with an assumptions section, and its 8px tablet gap is thin for gloved use. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick the 4px base with a 1.2 ratio, tie the choice to dense desktop tables and gloved tablet use, and treat Tailwind fairly: keep its spacing, drop its type scale. A wins narrowly because its system is more deliberate: 9 spacing steps that widen above 16px, a single set of 6 type roles, and two density modes that choose among the same tokens. B adds useful rules (tabular numerals, choosing the mode with `pointer: coarse`), but it uses nearly every 4px multiple up to 48 and keeps two parallel type scales.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick 4px/1.2, give implementable tokens, handle desktop and gloved-tablet density with explicit target sizes, and treat Tailwind fairly. B wins on rubric item 3 because it cuts spacing to 8 named steps and explains why it drops 20 and 40, while A lists 12 values that are close to every multiple. B's type scale only loosely follows 1.2, and it cites 28px rows but specifies 32px compact rows; A's dual-base type table is more precise. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick 4px with a 1.2 ratio, build on Tailwind for a stated reason, and handle desktop versus gloved-tablet use with density tokens and a minimum touch target of 48/56px. A gives a shorter, more deliberate set of 8 spacing steps and 6 type roles, and explains why it leaves some steps out. B lists 12 spacing values and two parallel type scales that include odd sizes such as 13, 29 and 33px, which makes it more complex. B is stronger on Tailwind specifics, but A fits the rubric's call for few, deliberate steps and brevity better. A has a small inconsistency: it says dense tables need 28px rows but specifies 32px.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both pick 4px/1.2 and give spacing, type and density tables a developer could implement. A's case against B contradicts itself: it calls a 32px row too loose, then uses 32px rows for desktop. B ties its numbers more directly to gloved use (48/56 targets, spacing between targets, pointer: coarse switching), treats Tailwind more fairly, and says the values need real-device testing, though it is slightly longer and has two more type steps. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick a 4px base with a 1.2 ratio and give density modes with 48/56px gloved tap targets. B has a shorter, more deliberate type scale and a more practical Tailwind plan (keep the keys, trim the theme). However, B calls 32px rows 'too loose' while using 32px rows for its own desktop mode, which undercuts its main argument against Dev B. A is tighter and internally consistent, and it ends with a sensible instruction to test with gloves and real tables, so it wins narrowly.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give plausible numbers, use a 68ch reading measure, scroll code and tables inside their own box, and bleed them to the screen edge on phones. A's CSS is tighter and more consistent: one shared grid serves both page types through span variables, values are tokenized, and it adds the fewest breakpoints its pages need. B explains its choices well, especially the code-width reasoning, but repeats the pricing grid, includes a non-standard `composes` line, and hard-codes several values (34rem, 4rem, 28rem) outside its tokens. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give plausible numbers (68ch measure, rem-based wrappers, a clamp() gutter, a root font bump on huge monitors) and handle code and tables well, with scrolling inside the block and edge-to-edge bleed on phones. A lets code use the full article column, which is a thoughtful touch, but its CSS has an invalid `composes:` line, a duplicated pricing block and several repeated magic numbers (4rem, 34rem, 28rem). B's CSS is cleaner and more token-driven, with three breakpoints and a clear split between the prose and wide containers, though its 4/8/12 span system is a little heavier than these pages strictly need.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B gives one consistent set of values: a shared 80rem page width, a 66ch measure and three breakpoints that are all actually used. Its docs-column math checks out (about 664px at 1024px and about 656px at 1280px), and its CSS mostly uses the tokens it names. A has a clever full/wide/content breakout grid and a strong table and code treatment, but it uses two page maximums (80rem and 90rem), hard-codes values like 90rem and 72rem, and lists a 40rem breakpoint it never uses. That weakens its 'one set of rules' claim, though B's 4/8/12 column scheme is a bit heavier than these pages need. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B wins narrowly. Its full/wide/content grid with named lines handles code blocks and tables better: they break out to a wider column and scroll inside it. It also covers very large monitors and mid-size screens explicitly. A is simpler and more consistent in its tokens, with one 80rem page width and no stray literals. B uses two page maximums (80rem and 90rem), hardcodes 72rem and 4rem, and adds fluid type and sticky table columns that the pages don't need.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give plausible values: a 68ch prose measure, a breakout grid for code and tables, scroll wrappers, and a docs shell with sidebar and table of contents. B builds more from its named tokens (the breakout width is calculated from them), says plainly that nothing grows past 1440px, and needs only three breakpoints, although its 4/8/12 column token is never used. A has good ideas, such as pricing that responds to its container, but it repeats magic numbers in the docs shell, uses five breakpoints plus font scaling, and has a bug: `.docs aside` hides the TOC on phones but not the `nav.sidebar`. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give plausible numbers, a 68ch measure, a breakout grid for code and tables, and scroll wrappers for wide content, and both stop growing at 1440px. A is more economical, with three breakpoints, and routes nearly all of its rules through named tokens, though it defines --layout-cols and never uses it. B uses more breakpoints, adds font scaling and container queries, and hard-codes the docs-shell widths and the feature and pricing gaps. B also has a small bug: its sidebar is a nav, but only aside elements are hidden, so the sidebar shows above the article on phones.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers fit within 120 words and both give purpose-based example names. Neither is fully paste-ready: A adds a note after the message, while B adds a preamble and a note. B wins on substance because it explicitly says to pick the nearest existing token, sets a concrete test for additions (a second screen or team needs it) and covers removals, which goes more directly at the one-off problem. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A is stronger on the substance. Its naming examples are all by role, it tells people to pick the nearest existing token, and its process has a real test (a second screen or team needs it) plus an owner and a step for removals. B is warmer, has no preamble and comes in under 120 words. But its `space-4`/`space-8` examples go against its own 'purpose, not value' rule, it never says what to use when something nearly fits, and it presents a made-up channel and weekly review as if they were real. Both wrap the message in commentary, and A also opens with a preamble, which costs it on item 1.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both messages fit under 120 words, but both wrap the message in a note to the user, and B's notes aren't separated from the message. A has a clear owner and review window, a friendly tone, and one weak example (`space-4` names a value). B has stronger role-based names and a useful 'second real use' test, but it opens with a scolding 'Please stop...' and 'Never', its 'keep it local' exception clashes with that opening, and its closing line is unclear. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both messages are under 120 words. Both also add meta text: A's placeholder note follows the message with no separator, while B's preamble and notes sit outside clear --- markers, so B's message is easier to copy out. A gives the sharper test (a new value needs a second real use) and clearer reuse guidance, but its opening ('Please stop…', 'Never') reads as scolding. B names an owner and a review window and sounds more collegial, though its examples `space-4` and `radius-md` name a value, not a purpose, which contradicts its own rule.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both messages fit within 120 words, but both include an intro and closing notes around the text to paste. B tells people to check whether the nearest token works and gives a clear test for additions: a second real use, plus why the closest token doesn't fit. A's "no time to wait" line suggests people can skip review, its opening "Please stop" sounds scolding, and its `space-4` example doesn't follow its own naming pattern. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A gives purpose-based example names throughout, says to try the nearest token first, and sets a clear test for additions (a second real use) with a named approver. B opens with a scolding "Please stop," includes the value-based example `space-4`, and its "no time to wait" clause leaves room for the one-off values the team wants to stop. Both messages fit in 120 words, but both answers add notes before and after the message that the user would have to remove before pasting.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep every value and class name, and both get the secondary button size right by computing its padding with calc() from the border width. B names its spacing steps (space-1 to space-6) rather than by pixel value, and puts the button padding in its own tokens. It also explains why it kept 12/14 and 18/20 as separate steps and what merging them would shift. A's spacing names are just the pixel values (--space-10), which is closer to describing appearance, though A openly says so. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers keep every class name and render the same pixels, and both build the secondary button's 9px/17px padding as base padding minus the border width with calc(). A's spacing names are steps on a scale (space-1 to space-6), which fits the rubric's request for role or step names. B's are pixel-value names (--space-10), which tie each name to a raw value, though B does say why. A also gives a reason for keeping 12/14 and 18/20 as separate steps and names the 1–2px shift that merging them would cause.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep every computed value, every class name and the 9px/17px border compensation (worked out as base padding minus border width), so they render the same. B's role names for radius and shadow are a bit better, but its ':root' comment says the colours are raw values used only through roles, and no role layer exists. B also leans on dark-mode framing nobody asked for. A is accurate, concise and does exactly what was asked, which gives it a narrow edge. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers make the same safe refactor: they turn every repeated value into a variable, keep each rendered value exactly as before, and work out the secondary button's 9px/17px padding from the base padding minus the border width. A's names fit the roles a little better (--radius-control, --font-size-control). But A's top comment talks about a separate set of role variables that doesn't exist, and its notes bring up dark mode twice, which nobody asked for. B's summary is tighter and more practical, with notes on the danger button keeping border: 0 and on why the hover colours stay as exact hex values.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A puts every repeated value into a variable, including spacing and font sizes, which the request specifically asked for. Each variable maps to exactly one original value, so nothing changes visually, and the variable names describe a role or a step on a scale. Answer B handles colors, radii and the secondary-button border math well, but it leaves spacing and font sizes as hard-coded numbers and uses button-only padding variables. That leaves less to reuse when building new components, even though B gives a sensible reason for the choice. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep every class name and computed value, and both derive the secondary button's padding with calc() so its size matches .btn. Rubric item 1 explicitly asks for spacing and font sizes as variables: B tokenizes them with step and role names, while A leaves them as literals and gives a reason. B also notes which spacing steps could later be merged and what that would cost, without snapping anything.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers show three nearly identical side-by-side themes. In both, the high-contrast card gets taller because its borders are thicker, so the spacing shifts slightly. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): The two answers are nearly identical: each shows three themes side by side, a well-judged dark palette with lighter green and coral amounts, and a high-contrast theme with heavier borders, a darker button and +/− signs on amounts. A wins narrowly because its secondary text is larger and easier to read, and its transactions include category labels. B's small Income/Spent labels and dates are a little faint and small, especially on the dark card. In both answers the thicker high-contrast borders make that card slightly taller, so the layout is not perfectly identical across themes. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): The two answers are nearly the same: three side-by-side cards render the same screen, the light theme matches the brief, the dark palettes are considered with lighter greens and corals, and +/− signs carry meaning beyond color. A's high-contrast theme puts heavier borders on the transaction list, while B's makes the amounts bolder and its secondary labels a little more legible. In both, the high-contrast card is slightly taller than the others, and neither has a meaningful advantage overall.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers use token-driven themes with a well-adjusted dark palette and a stronger high-contrast variant, and in both the light theme matches the brief. B goes further: direction icons and signs separate gains from spending in addition to color, and its high-contrast button has an added border. The only drawback is that B's cards are slightly cut off at the bottom of the screenshot, though the button is still fully visible. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers render the three themes side by side with matching layouts, a faithful light theme, a well-tuned dark palette with lighter green and coral, and a high-contrast theme with heavier borders and darker tones. A edges ahead because its direction-arrow icons tell gains from spending without relying on color or the sign alone, and its high-contrast button has a stronger outline. A's panels are slightly clipped at the bottom of the screenshot, while B's fit fully, and B's high-contrast button lacks an outline.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers stay on-brand: they use zero radius, express depth with rules and an optional zero-blur hard offset, keep motion minimal and respect reduced motion. A edges ahead because it treats circles as a named exception rather than adding a token, defines raised and overlay clearly, and picks an ink focus ring because a tomato ring would disappear on tomato elements, which B suggests. B's motion is slightly more on-brand (linear easing, colour changes only), but A's single fade curve is still restrained. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep radius at zero, build depth from rules, and keep motion minimal with reduced-motion handling, so they are close. B wins narrowly: it maps raised and overlay to named elevation roles and gives one complete block of CSS ready to paste. A's motion fits the brand slightly better, since it uses linear easing for color changes only, while B adds a cubic-bezier curve and a raw-to-semantic border layer that repeats the same values.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers respect the flat, square brand: radius is zero with a circle exception, depth comes from thick rules and a zero-blur offset, and motion stays minimal with reduced-motion handling. B wins because it gives complete paste-ready CSS, including the reduced-motion media query. It also explains why overlays need the offset, offers a no-shadow alternative, and states which properties may transition. A is nearly as good, but its elevation tokens are a little muddled (elevation-2 just aliases elevation-1) and its reduced-motion rule is described rather than written out. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers follow the brand closely: zero radius with a justified circle exception, depth from borders plus a zero-blur offset, minimal motion with reduced-motion handling, and an explicit list of what is left out. A edges ahead because it gives a complete paste-ready CSS block with a raw layer and a semantic layer, a clear table of what makes raised and overlay elements different, and a no-shadow alternative for overlays. B's `--elevation-2` simply aliases `--elevation-1`, with the offset in a separate token, which makes it a bit less tidy and less ready to paste.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers keep radius at zero, show depth with black rules instead of blur, and keep motion close to nothing, so on the core brief they're nearly equal.
